title: DiffPTS: Rethinking Diffusion ELBO for Probabilistic Time Series Forecasting

paper.title: DiffPTS: Rethinking Diffusion ELBO for Probabilistic Time Series Forecasting
paper.abstract: Abstract Probabilistic time series forecasting requires modeling and predicting complex and time-varying distributions. Recently, Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Model (DDPM)-based approaches have shown promise by equipping the diffusion process with pretrained mean and variance estimators to accommodate distributional shift. However, these methods typically follow the standard DDPM framework and consider only partial components of the evidence lower bound (ELBO), treating the training of estimators as designed regression tasks separate from the variational inference framework. To address this, we rethink the ELBO under the Location-Scale Noise Model (LSNM) and find that it naturally induces a Gaussian negative log likelihood objective for the estimators and inherently defines a joint training objective that unifies recent diffusion paradigms for probabilistic forecasting. Building on this principled ELBO reformulation, we propose DiffPTS, a general framework that enables end-to-end optimization of all components within the ELBO. Across multiple benchmarks, DiffPTS consistently outperforms recent models, achieving state-of-the-art performance with an average CRPS/MSE reduction of over 14.53%/16.55% compared to existing diffusion-based methods. The code is available at https://github.com/wwy155/DiffPTS .

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Probabilistic time series forecasting (PTSF) has become increasingly crucial in various real-world applications ranging from financial risk management [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] to climate prediction [ 4 , 5 ] . In particular, PTSF aims to effectively model the conditional distribution p ⁡ ( 𝐘 | 𝐗 ) p(\mathbf{Y}|\mathbf{X}) of future outcomes 𝐘 \mathbf{Y} given historical observations 𝐗 \mathbf{X} [ 6 ] . Given the dynamic nature of time series data, the fundamental challenge lies in accurately capturing complex and time-varying distributions [ 7 , 8 , 9 ] . In recent years, Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models (DDPMs) [ 10 , 11 ] have emerged as a powerful framework for modeling complex distributions, inspiring their growing adoption in probabilistic forecasting scenarios [ 12 , 13 , 14 ] . At their core, standard DDPMs optimize the Evidence Lower Bound (ELBO) to learn the data distribution by introducing a denoising network ϵ θ \epsilon_{\theta} that learns to predict the noise added during the forward diffusion process, enabling tractable variational inference from a fixed Gaussian endpoint p ⁡ ( 𝐘 T ) = 𝒩 ⁡ ( 𝟎 , 𝐈 ) p(\mathbf{Y}_{T})=\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{I}) . However, conventional DDPMs often fail in accurate probabilistic forecasting due to distributional shifts [ 8 , 15 , 16 ] . To address this limitation, recent approaches have proposed introducing adaptive mean and variance estimators ( f ϕ ​ ( 𝐗 ) f_{\phi}(\mathbf{X}) , OPEN g ψ ​ ( 𝐗 ) ) g_{\psi}(\mathbf{X})) into the diffusion process, either by designing a new residual-based denoising target ( 𝐘 − f ϕ ​ ( 𝐗 ) ) / g ψ ​ ( 𝐗 ) (\mathbf{Y}-f_{\phi}(\mathbf{X}))/g_{\psi}(\mathbf{X}) or by modifying the reverse diffusion endpoint to follow 𝒩 ⁡ ( f ϕ ​ ( 𝐗 ) , g ψ ​ ( 𝐗 ) ) \mathcal{N}(f_{\phi}(\mathbf{X}),g_{\psi}(\mathbf{X})) to accommodate distributional changes [ 8 , 17 ] , which have shown promising results [ 18 , 19 ] . Typically, these advancements follow the standard diffusion training paradigm, and the training of f ϕ f_{\phi} and g ψ g_{\psi} is conducted in separate pretraining stages or as auxiliary regression tasks by designing various targets for f ϕ f_{\phi} and g ψ g_{\psi} (e.g., NsDiff [ 8 ] uses a future sliding variance target for g ψ g_{\psi} ). These diverse design choices for training f ϕ f_{\phi} and g ψ g_{\psi} raise a critical question: How should f ϕ f_{\phi} and g ψ g_{\psi} be trained to best align with the DDPM within the variational inference framework? Motivated by this question, we rethink the ELBO and surprisingly find that when introducing adaptive estimators into the DDPM, crucial ELBO terms that were previously treated as constants become non-negligible and require explicit joint optimization. Specifically, the reconstruction non-denoising terms and prior matching terms must be strictly optimized to achieve a tight variational bound. Figure 1: Figure 1 illustrates the comparison of DDPM-based models on the ETTm1 dataset. The left panel displays the prediction intervals, while the right panel shows the corresponding endpoint distributions for TimeGrad, NsDiff, and DiffPTS (ours), respectively. Both TimeGrad and NsDiff utilize the standard ELBO objective from DDPM, whereas DiffPTS reformulates the ELBO to enable end-to-end training within a unified framework. Figure 1 presents a comparative analysis on the ETTm1 (Electricity Transformer Temperature, minutes) dataset, showcasing estimated prediction intervals (Left) and endpoint distributions (Right) across three diffusion-based models: TimeGrad [ 13 ] , NsDiff [ 8 ] , and our proposed DiffPTS. TimeGrad [ 13 ] follows the conventional DDPM framework with a fixed Gaussian prior, which fails to capture the temporal variability inherent in time series data. While NsDiff allows for dynamic mean and variance estimation by introducing the adaptive endpoint 𝒩 ⁡ ( f ⁡ ( 𝐗 ) , g ⁡ ( 𝐗 ) ) \mathcal{N}(f(\mathbf{X}),g(\mathbf{X})) , f ϕ , g ψ f_{\phi},g_{\psi} are considered as priors pretrained with designed losses that may not be inherently aligned with the diffusion process; as a result, the sliding variance target for g ψ g_{\psi} leads to an over-estimation in the uncertainty. Based on this observation, we rethink the ELBO under the Location-Scale Noise Model (LSNM) with estimators f ϕ , g ψ f_{\phi},g_{\psi} , and find that all three terms (reconstruction, denoise, prior matching) in the ELBO inherently require strict optimization, whereas two of them are largely discarded in recent methods. By reformulating the ELBO to explicitly incorporate these components, we establish a unified optimization objective that seamlessly integrates the training of estimators with the core diffusion training process. As in Figure 1 , DiffPTS optimizes these key components under the guidance of the core ELBO that is inherently required by the diffusion process, leading to a more accurate estimation (More explanation is given in Figure 3 ). In summary, our contributions are: 1) We identify a critical theoretical puzzle in recent advances for diffusion-based probabilistic forecasting: while trainable parameters are introduced to model distributional shift, they are not optimized within the diffusion ELBO framework. 2) We reformulate the diffusion ELBO to properly incorporate the introduced mean and variance estimators. Our analysis reveals that the ELBO inherently specifies a Gaussian negative log likelihood (NLL) objective for both estimators, indicating that prior approaches relying on manually designed targets may be fundamentally misaligned with the diffusion process. Moreover, we show that the ELBO provides a unified objective for both residual-based and endpoint-based methods. 3) Based on the reformulated ELBO, we propose DiffPTS, a novel end-to-end diffusion framework for PTSF. Extensive experiments demonstrate that DiffPTS consistently yields significant improvements in probabilistic forecasting performance. Notably, it outperforms previous diffusion-based baselines by over 14.53%/16.55% in CRPS/MSE across nine benchmarks, highlighting the importance of a full ELBO formulation.

sections.heading: 2.1 Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Model
sections.text: Diffusion probabilistic models [ 11 ] define a generative process by modeling the data distribution p ⁡ ( 𝐘 0 ) p(\mathbf{Y}_{0}) as the marginal of a joint distribution over a sequence of latent variables 𝐘 1 , … , 𝐘 T \mathbf{Y}_{1},\dots,\mathbf{Y}_{T} : p ( 𝐘 0 ) := ∫ p ( 𝐘 0 : T ) d 𝐘 1 : T p(\mathbf{Y}_{0}):=\int p(\mathbf{Y}_{0:T})\,d\mathbf{Y}_{1:T} . Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models (DDPMs) [ 10 ] construct the diffusion process based on a Markovian chain [ 20 ] : p ( 𝐘 0 : T ) := p ( 𝐘 T ) ∏ t = 1 T p ( 𝐘 t − 1 ∣ 𝐘 t ) p(\mathbf{Y}_{0:T}):=p(\mathbf{Y}_{T})\prod_{t=1}^{T}p(\mathbf{Y}_{t-1}\mid\mathbf{Y}_{t}) . In DDPM, the endpoint distribution is fixed to a Gaussian prior, i.e., p ⁡ ( 𝐘 T ) = 𝒩 ⁡ ( 𝟎 , 𝐈 ) p(\mathbf{Y}_{T})=\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{I}) . The model comprises two complementary processes: a forward process that progressively corrupts data by adding Gaussian noise, and a reverse (or denoising ) process that learns to recover the original data by iteratively removing noise [ 21 ] . The forward process is defined as: q ( 𝐘 1 : T ∣ 𝐘 0 ) \displaystyle q(\mathbf{Y}_{1:T}\mid\mathbf{Y}_{0}) : = ∏ t = 1 T q ⁡ ( 𝐘 t ∣ 𝐘 t − 1 ) , q ⁡ ( 𝐘 t ∣ 𝐘 t − 1 ) := 𝒩 ⁡ ( 𝐘 t , 1 − β t ​ 𝐘 t − 1 , β t ​ 𝐈 ) , \displaystyle:=\prod_{t=1}^{T}q(\mathbf{Y}_{t}\mid\mathbf{Y}_{t-1}),\quad q(\mathbf{Y}_{t}\mid\mathbf{Y}_{t-1}):=\mathcal{N}\big(\mathbf{Y}_{t};\sqrt{1-\beta_{t}}\,\mathbf{Y}_{t-1},\,\beta_{t}\mathbf{I}\big), (1) where β t ∈ ( 0 , 1 ) \beta_{t}\in(0,1) is a pre-specified noise schedule that controls the variance of added noise at each step. The reverse process involves denoising 𝐘 T \mathbf{Y}_{T} back to 𝐘 0 \mathbf{Y}_{0} and is parameterized by a learnable Gaussian transition kernel: p θ ​ ( 𝐘 t − 1 | 𝐘 t ) p_{\theta}(\mathbf{Y}_{t-1}|\mathbf{Y}_{t}) : p θ ​ ( 𝐘 t − 1 | 𝐘 t ) := 𝒩 ⁡ ( 𝐘 t − 1 , 𝝁 θ ​ ( 𝐘 t , t ) , 𝝈 θ ​ ( 𝐘 t , t ) ) , p_{\theta}(\mathbf{Y}_{t-1}|\mathbf{Y}_{t}):=\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{Y}_{t-1};\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\theta}(\mathbf{Y}_{t},t),\boldsymbol{\sigma}_{\theta}(\mathbf{Y}_{t},t)), (2) 𝝁 θ ​ ( 𝐘 t , t ) := 1 α t ​ ( 𝐘 t − β t 1 − α ¯ t ​ ϵ θ ​ ( 𝐘 t , t ) ) , 𝝈 θ ​ ( 𝐘 t , t ) = 1 − α ¯ t − 1 1 − α ¯ t ​ β t ​ 𝐈 , \boldsymbol{\mu}_{\theta}(\mathbf{Y}_{t},t):=\frac{1}{\sqrt{\alpha_{t}}}(\mathbf{Y}_{t}-\frac{\beta_{t}}{\sqrt{1-\bar{\alpha}_{t}}}\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{\theta}(\mathbf{Y}_{t},t)),\quad\boldsymbol{\sigma}_{\theta}(\mathbf{Y}_{t},t)=\frac{1-\bar{\alpha}_{t-1}}{1-\bar{\alpha}_{t}}\beta_{t}\mathbf{I}, (3) where α t := 1 − β t \alpha_{t}:=1-\beta_{t} , α ¯ t := ∏ i = 1 t α i \bar{\alpha}_{t}:=\prod_{i=1}^{t}\alpha_{i} , and ϵ θ ​ ( ⋅ , t ) \boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{\theta}(\cdot,t) denotes a neural network trained to predict the noise added at step t t . Training in DDPM is performed by maximizing a variational lower bound on the log-likelihood, known as the Evidence Lower Bound (ELBO) [ 15 , 22 ] : ELBO = 𝔼 q ⁡ ( 𝐘 1 ∣ 𝐘 0 ) [ log p θ ( 𝐘 0 ∣ 𝐘 1 ) ] − D KL ( q ( 𝐘 T ∣ 𝐘 0 ) ∥ p ( 𝐘 T ) ) \displaystyle=\;\mathbb{E}_{q(\mathbf{Y}_{1}\mid\mathbf{Y}_{0})}\left[\log p_{\theta}(\mathbf{Y}_{0}\mid\mathbf{Y}_{1})\right]-D_{\text{KL}}\big(q(\mathbf{Y}_{T}\mid\mathbf{Y}_{0})\,\|\,p(\mathbf{Y}_{T})\big) − ∑ t = 2 T 𝔼 q ⁡ ( 𝐘 t ∣ 𝐘 0 ) [ D KL ( q ( 𝐘 t − 1 ∣ 𝐘 t , 𝐘 0 ) ∥ p θ ( 𝐘 t − 1 ∣ 𝐘 t ) ) ] . \displaystyle-\sum_{t=2}^{T}\mathbb{E}_{q(\mathbf{Y}_{t}\mid\mathbf{Y}_{0})}\left[D_{\text{KL}}\big(q(\mathbf{Y}_{t-1}\mid\mathbf{Y}_{t},\mathbf{Y}_{0})\,\|\,p_{\theta}(\mathbf{Y}_{t-1}\mid\mathbf{Y}_{t})\big)\right]. (4) The first, second, and third terms in the ELBO objective are commonly referred to as the reconstruction , prior matching , and denoising terms, respectively. Crucially, in standard DDPM, the prior matching term is a KL divergence between two fixed distributions, which can be analytically computed and thus ignored during optimization [ 23 , 24 ] . Similarly, the reconstruction term involving q ⁡ ( 𝐘 0 | 𝐘 1 ) q(\mathbf{Y}_{0}|\mathbf{Y}_{1}) corresponds to a fixed distribution and can be reduced to the denoising term at t = 1 t=1 . As noted in [ 10 ] , p θ ​ ( ⋅ ) p_{\theta}(\cdot) can be reparameterized such that the dominant contribution to the loss arises from predicting the noise injected during the forward process. At inference time, new samples are generated by first drawing 𝐘 T ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 𝟎 , 𝐈 ) \mathbf{Y}_{T}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{I}) and then iteratively applying the learned reverse process from t = T t=T down to t = 1 t=1 .

sections.heading: 2.2 Probabilistic Time Series Forecasting
sections.text: Given a historical multivariate time series sample 𝐗 ∈ ℝ N × D \mathbf{X}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times D} , where N N denotes the look-back window length and D D the number of variables, the goal of probabilistic forecasting is to characterize the conditional distribution of the future trajectory p ( 𝐘 ) = { p ( 𝐲 1 ) , p ( 𝐲 2 ) , … , p ( 𝐲 M ) | 𝐲 ∈ ℝ D } p(\mathbf{Y})=\{p(\mathbf{y}_{1}),p(\mathbf{y}_{2}),...,p(\mathbf{y}_{M})|\mathbf{y}\in\mathbb{R}^{D}\} , where M M is the future window size. In this context, this DDPM framework is naturally extended to conditional DDPM [ 25 ] , which incorporates past observations 𝐗 \mathbf{X} as an additional conditioning variable, and the conditional DDPM is formulated as: p θ ( 𝐘 0 : T | 𝐗 ) := p ( 𝐘 T | 𝐗 ) ∏ t = 1 T p θ ( 𝐘 t − 1 ∣ 𝐘 t , 𝐗 ) , p_{\theta}(\mathbf{Y}_{0:T}|\mathbf{X}):=p(\mathbf{Y}_{T}|\mathbf{X})\prod_{t=1}^{T}p_{\theta}(\mathbf{Y}_{t-1}\mid\mathbf{Y}_{t},\mathbf{X}), (6) p θ ​ ( 𝐘 t − 1 ∣ 𝐘 t , 𝐗 ) := 𝒩 ⁡ ( 𝐘 t − 1 , 𝝁 θ ​ ( 𝐘 t , 𝐗 , t ) , 𝝈 θ ​ ( 𝐘 t , 𝐗 , t ) ) . p_{\theta}(\mathbf{Y}_{t-1}\mid\mathbf{Y}_{t},\mathbf{X}):=\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{Y}_{t-1};\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\theta}(\mathbf{Y}_{t},\mathbf{X},t),\boldsymbol{\sigma}_{\theta}(\mathbf{Y}_{t},\mathbf{X},t)). (7) The reverse transition is typically parameterized by incorporating an additional conditioning input to the denoising network: ϵ θ ​ ( ⋅ , t , 𝐗 ) \boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{\theta}(\cdot,t;\mathbf{X}) . Beyond this parameterization, several studies [ 12 , 13 , 14 ] have proposed mechanisms to incorporate various conditional information, e.g., mixed historical codes, into the reverse process to better guide the denoising function. Notably, both the ELBO (Equation ( 4 )) and the simplified denoising loss (Equation ( 5 )) retain their original form in these methods. Nevertheless, PTSF poses unique challenges due to strong temporal dependencies [ 26 , 27 , 28 ] , non-stationarity [ 7 , 29 ] , and input-dependent uncertainty [ 21 , 30 ] . While diffusion models have shown promise in this domain [ 12 , 13 ] , the conventional paradigm, diffusing raw observations 𝐘 \mathbf{Y} toward a standard Gaussian prior, often overlooks the input-dependent nature of predictive uncertainty [ 31 , 32 ] . To better align with the forecasting task, recent works propose to reformulate the diffusion process by leveraging a deterministic predictor f ϕ ​ ( 𝐗 ) f_{\phi}(\mathbf{X}) and uncertainty estimator g ψ ​ ( 𝐗 ) g_{\psi}(\mathbf{X}) trained on the context 𝐗 \mathbf{X} . For instance, some methods diffuse the residual ( 𝐘 − f ϕ ​ ( 𝐗 ) ) / g ψ ​ ( 𝐗 ) (\mathbf{Y}-f_{\phi}(\mathbf{X}))/g_{\psi}(\mathbf{X}) instead of 𝐘 \mathbf{Y} itself [ 16 , 17 ] , while others replace the standard prior with an adaptive endpoint 𝒩 ⁡ ( f ϕ ​ ( 𝐗 ) , g ψ ​ ( 𝐗 ) ) \mathcal{N}(f_{\phi}(\mathbf{X}),g_{\psi}(\mathbf{X})) [ 8 , 33 ] . These designs implicitly assume that the diffusion endpoint 𝐘 T \mathbf{Y}_{T} follows a Location-scale noise model (LSNM) [ 8 ] , where both the mean and uncertainty are input-dependent: 𝐘 T = f ϕ ​ ( 𝐗 ) + g ψ ​ ( 𝐗 ) ⊙ 𝜼 , \mathbf{Y}_{T}=f_{\phi}(\mathbf{X})+\sqrt{g_{\psi}(\mathbf{X})}\odot\boldsymbol{\eta}, (8) where 𝜼 ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 𝟎 , 𝐈 ) \boldsymbol{\eta}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{I}) , and ⊙ \odot denotes element-wise multiplication (all operations are element-wise unless indicated). Here, f ϕ ​ ( 𝐗 ) ∈ ℝ M × D f_{\phi}(\mathbf{X})\in\mathbb{R}^{M\times D} estimates the conditional mean 𝔼 ⁡ [ 𝐘 ∣ 𝐗 ] \mathbb{E}[\mathbf{Y}\mid\mathbf{X}] , while g ψ ​ ( 𝐗 ) ∈ ℝ > 0 M × D g_{\psi}(\mathbf{X})\in\mathbb{R}_{>0}^{M\times D} models input-dependent uncertainty, both can be interpreted as prior without parameters.

sections.heading: 3 Discussion & Methodology
sections.text: In this section, we rethink the foundational ELBO of recent diffusion-based methods for probabilistic time series forecasting. We summarize existing approaches and find that, despite introducing auxiliary estimators, these components are not dictated by the standard ELBO and are instead added heuristically. Based on this observation, we argue that a proper variational objective should explicitly govern the form and role of these estimators. To this end, we derive a corrected evidence lower bound that imposes precise requirements on the introduced estimators, ensuring a tighter variational bound. Building on this formulation, we present DiffPTS , a novel probabilistic forecasting framework trained in an end-to-end joint optimization scheme and we describe its training and sampling algorithms.

sections.heading: 3.1 The Missing Puzzle of The ELBO
sections.text: Recent diffusion-based approaches for probabilistic time series forecasting have achieved notable success. To realize these designs, all existing methods require additional estimators beyond the core denoising network ϵ θ \epsilon_{\theta} , i.e., a deterministic forecaster f ϕ ​ ( 𝐗 ) f_{\phi}(\mathbf{X}) or a variance estimator g ψ ​ ( 𝐗 ) g_{\psi}(\mathbf{X}) . However, a critical question remains largely unexamined: when these methods introduce external components (e.g., a base forecaster f ϕ f_{\phi} or a variance estimator g ψ g_{\psi} ), are these components theoretically grounded in the variational objective, or are they heuristically appended without proper alignment to the ELBO? Notably, despite their empirical effectiveness, none of these methods derive a revised evidence lower bound that accounts for the input-dependent transformation implied by the LSNM. Consequently, the auxiliary estimators are trained via ad-hoc supervised losses (e.g., MSE for f ϕ f_{\phi} or sliding-window variance for g ψ g_{\psi} ) that are decoupled from the diffusion likelihood objective.

sections.heading: 4.1 Experiment Setup
sections.text: Datasets . Following previous work [ 8 , 33 ] , we evaluate on nine real-world datasets: ETT {h1, h2, m1, m2}, Electricity (ECL), Influenza-like Illness (ILI), Exchange Rate (EXR), Traffic, and Solar Energy (Solar). All experiments adopt a input sequence length of 168 time steps, ILI uses 32 prediction steps, and other datasets follow 192 prediction steps. Data splits follow domain conventions: ETT datasets use 12/4/4-month partitions for training, validation, and testing; all other datasets employ a chronological 7:1:2 split ratio. We provide dataset details in Appendix B.1 . Baselines . We select eight recent strong PTSF baselines for comparison, including TimeGrad [ 13 ] , CSDI [ 12 ] , TimeDiff [ 14 ] , TMDM [ 33 ] , DiffusionTS [ 35 ] , D3U [ 16 ] , RDIT [ 17 ] , NsDiff [ 8 ] . Specifically, TimeGrad, CSDI, TimeDiff, DiffusionTS follow the standard diffusion paradigm; TMDM, D3U, RDIT, NsDiff introduce estimators into diffusion process through two phases pretraining. Implementation . All experiments are conducted under popular long-term multivariate probabilistic forecasting settings [ 8 , 33 ] . We run all experiments with seeds { 1 , 2 , 3 } \{1,2,3\} for 10 epochs and select the best model based on the validation performance for final test evaluation. The learning rate is set to 0.001, batch size to 32, and the number of timesteps T = 20 T=20 , consistent with prior work [ 8 , 13 ] . We employ a linear noise schedule with β 1 = 10 − 4 \beta^{1}=10^{-4} and β T = 0.02 \beta^{T}=0.02 , in line with the setup used in conventional DDPM [ 10 ] . We use Adam optimizer [ 36 ] and the experiments were all performed using an NVIDIA RTX A6000 GPU. In inference, we generate 100 samples to estimate the distribution [ 37 , 38 ] . For the baseline models, we utilize their default parameters. For implementation of f ϕ f_{\phi} and g ψ g_{\psi} , we follow previous work [ 8 , 33 ] to use Non-stationary Transformer [ 39 ] and a three-layer linear model [ 40 , 41 ] , respectively. More details are provided in Appendix B.2 . Metrics . Following prior work’s metric settings [ 8 , 13 , 33 ] , we use Continuous Ranked Probability Score (CRPS) [ 42 ] and mean square error (MSE) to validate the performance of the estimated uncertainty quantification and point forecasting performance. For both metrics, smaller values indicate better performance. Detailed formula is provided in Appendix B.3 .

sections.heading: 4.2 Main Experiments
sections.text: The experimental results are presented in Table 2 . DiffPTS demonstrates state-of-the-art performance across all nine real-world datasets in probabilistic time series forecasting, outperforming all competitive baselines including recent diffusion-based models such as NsDiff, RDIT, and D3U. On the ECL dataset, DiffPTS reduces CRPS by 24.8% (from 0.290 to 0.218) and MSE by 13.9% (from 0.209 to 0.180) compared to NsDiff. Similarly, on the Traffic dataset, DiffPTS achieves a 28.6% reduction in CRPS (from 0.378 to 0.270) and a 28.4% reduction in MSE (from 0.637 to 0.456). The results underscore the importance of optimizing the complete ELBO rather than relying on simplified denoising objectives. We provide results with two additional metrics in Appendix D.1 . This precise distributional modeling capability underscores DiffPTS’ effectiveness in learning time series distribution.

sections.heading: 5 Conclusion
sections.text: In this paper, we rethink the ELBO for diffusion-based probabilistic time series forecasting under the location-scale noise model. We show that the full ELBO naturally induces a Gaussian negative log-likelihood objective for adaptive mean and variance estimators, unifying recent methods and revealing that key terms are often overlooked. Based on this, we propose DiffPTS, an end-to-end framework that jointly optimizes all ELBO components. Experiments demonstrate consistent improvements over existing approaches, with plug-in enhancements surpassing state-of-the-art results. Limitation & Future work Our work focuses on the optimization objective rather than network architecture design; we do not investigate what architectural choices are best suited for modeling in the proposed framework. Future work could explore architecture-aware co-design of estimators and the diffusion process, extend the framework for faster inference, or incorporate domain-specific inductive biases for improved calibration and scalability. See Appendix E for further analyses.

sections.heading: A.4 Convergence Rate
sections.text: Lee et al. [ 15 ] demonstrates that the Hessian matrix of a data-dependent Gaussian prior 𝒩 ⁡ ( μ , Σ ) \mathcal{N}(\mu,\Sigma) has a condition number of at least 1. This result naturally extends to our setting. Specifically, under mild constraints and assuming ϵ θ \epsilon_{\theta} is a linear function, Lee et al. [ 15 ] proves that: min θ ⁡ L ⁡ ( 𝝁 , 𝚺 , 𝐘 0 , θ ) ≤ min θ ⁡ L ⁡ ( 𝟎 , 𝐈 , 𝐘 0 , θ ) . \min_{\theta}L(\boldsymbol{\mu},\boldsymbol{\Sigma},\mathbf{Y}_{0};\theta)\leq\min_{\theta}L(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{I},\mathbf{Y}_{0};\theta). This inequality indicates that a simple model suffices to represent the mean of q ⁡ ( 𝐘 t − 1 | 𝐘 t ) q(\mathbf{Y}_{t-1}|\mathbf{Y}_{t}) under a data-dependent prior, whereas achieving comparable precision with an isotropic covariance prior ( 𝟎 , 𝐈 \mathbf{0},\mathbf{I} ) requires a more complex model. Consequently, optimization under the data-dependent prior achieves the optimal condition number of 1 for the Hessian matrix of the loss function, yielding the fastest possible convergence rate.

sections.heading: B.3 Metrics
sections.text: We adopt the following standard metrics to evaluate model performance: Mean Absolute Error (MAE) measures the average magnitude of absolute prediction errors: MAE = 1 M ​ D ​ ∑ i = 1 M ∑ j = 1 D | 𝐘 i , j − 𝐘 ^ i , j | , \text{MAE}=\frac{1}{MD}\sum_{i=1}^{M}\sum_{j=1}^{D}|\mathbf{Y}_{i,j}-\hat{\mathbf{Y}}_{i,j}|, where 𝐘 i , j \mathbf{Y}_{i,j} and 𝐘 ^ i , j \hat{\mathbf{Y}}_{i,j} denote the ground-truth and predicted values at the i i -th future step of the j j -th variate, M M is the prediction length, and D D is the number of variates. Both MAE and MSE are averaged over all test samples. Mean Squared Error (MSE) quantifies the average squared deviation between predictions and ground truth, penalizing larger errors more heavily: MSE = 1 M ​ D ​ ∑ i = 1 M ∑ j = 1 D ( 𝐘 i , j − 𝐘 ^ i , j ) 2 . \text{MSE}=\frac{1}{MD}\sum_{i=1}^{M}\sum_{j=1}^{D}(\mathbf{Y}_{i,j}-\hat{\mathbf{Y}}_{i,j})^{2}. CRPS. The continuous ranked probability score (CRPS) [ 42 ] quantifies the discrepancy between a predictive cumulative distribution function (CDF) F F and an observed outcome x x via CRPS ( F , x ) = ∫ ℝ ( F ( z ) − 𝕀 { x ≤ z } ) 2 d z , \operatorname{CRPS}(F,x)=\int_{\mathbb{R}}\bigl(F(z)-\mathbb{I}\{x\leq z\}\bigr)^{2}\,\mathrm{d}z, (59) where 𝕀 ​ { ⋅ } \mathbb{I}\{\cdot\} denotes the indicator function. In practice, when F F is approximated by its empirical counterpart F ^ ( z ) = 1 S ∑ s = 1 S 𝕀 { x 0 , s ≤ z } \hat{F}(z)=\frac{1}{S}\sum_{s=1}^{S}\mathbb{I}\{x^{0,s}\leq z\} constructed from S S samples x 0 , s ∼ F x^{0,s}\sim F , the CRPS can be estimated directly from the generated trajectories. In our experiments, we use S = 100 S=100 samples to approximate F F . QICE. The Quantile Interval Calibration Error (QICE) [ 34 ] quantifies the mismatch between the empirical coverage of predicted quantile intervals (QIs) and their nominal target coverage. Specifically, the predictive distribution is partitioned into I I non-overlapping, equal-probability quantile intervals, each assigned a nominal coverage of 1 / I 1/I . QICE then measures the average absolute deviation between the observed frequency of ground-truth values falling within each interval and the ideal coverage 1 / I 1/I . Formally, let y ^ n low m \hat{y}_{n}^{\text{low}_{m}} and y ^ n high m \hat{y}_{n}^{\text{high}_{m}} denote the lower and upper bounds of the m m -th quantile interval for the n n -th sample. The empirical coverage of the m m -th interval is given by r m = 1 N ∑ n = 1 N 𝕀 { y ^ n low m ≤ y n ≤ y ^ n high m } , r_{m}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^{N}\mathbb{I}\left\{\hat{y}_{n}^{\text{low}_{m}}\leq y_{n}\leq\hat{y}_{n}^{\text{high}_{m}}\right\}, where 𝕀 ​ { ⋅ } \mathbb{I}\{\cdot\} is the indicator function. QICE is defined as QICE := 1 I ​ ∑ m = 1 I | r m − 1 I | . \operatorname{QICE}:=\frac{1}{I}\sum_{m=1}^{I}\left|r_{m}-\frac{1}{I}\right|. (60) Under perfect calibration (i.e., when the predicted distribution coincides with the true data-generating distribution), we expect r m ≈ 1 / I r_{m}\approx 1/I for all m m , resulting in QICE → 0 \operatorname{QICE}\to 0 . Following Li et al. [ 33 ] , we use I = 10 I=10 equal-sized decile-based intervals to compute QICE.

Our proposed DiffPTS framework demonstrates consistent state-of-the-art performance. NsDiff demonstrates competitive QICE values on specific datasets like ETTh2 and ILI. These concrete results confirm that our principled ELBO reformulation serves as a powerful, architecture-agnostic plug-in module that can significantly enhance the probabilistic forecasting capability of diverse diffusion frameworks. sections.heading: E.1 On the LSNM Assumption and the Diagonal Covariance
sections.text: Following prior work [ 34 , 8 ] , the LSNM is often written directly on the target as 𝐘 = f ϕ ​ ( 𝐗 ) + g ψ ​ ( 𝐗 ) ⊙ 𝜼 \mathbf{Y}=f_{\phi}(\mathbf{X})+\sqrt{g_{\psi}(\mathbf{X})}\odot\boldsymbol{\eta} . Strictly speaking, however, in the diffusion models considered here the LSNM specifies the endpoint of the diffusion process rather than the final prediction, i.e., p ⁡ ( 𝐘 T ∣ 𝐗 ) = 𝒩 ⁡ ( f ϕ ​ ( 𝐗 ) , g ψ ​ ( 𝐗 ) ) p(\mathbf{Y}_{T}\mid\mathbf{X})=\mathcal{N}(f_{\phi}(\mathbf{X}),g_{\psi}(\mathbf{X})) as stated in Equation ( 8 ). The forward process in Equation ( 9 ) is constructed such that q ⁡ ( 𝐘 T ∣ 𝐘 0 , 𝐗 ) q(\mathbf{Y}_{T}\mid\mathbf{Y}_{0},\mathbf{X}) approaches this endpoint as α ¯ T \bar{\alpha}_{T} decreases, which is why the assumption is commonly stated on 𝐘 \mathbf{Y} itself. The diagonal Gaussian with covariance diag ​ ( g ψ ​ ( 𝐗 ) ) \mathrm{diag}(g_{\psi}(\mathbf{X})) therefore only initializes the generative process. The final predictive distribution is the full reverse process p θ ​ ( 𝐘 0 ∣ 𝐗 ) p_{\theta}(\mathbf{Y}_{0}\mid\mathbf{X}) , whose transitions are conditioned on the entire history 𝐗 \mathbf{X} and on all coordinates of 𝐘 t \mathbf{Y}_{t} and iteratively refine the sample. It is therefore not restricted to a diagonal Gaussian, and dependencies across time steps and variates can be captured through the reverse chain. A diagonal endpoint is also the standard setting of all compared methods, namely DDPM, NsDiff, TMDM, RDIT, and D3U. Explicitly modeling the full conditional covariance within the ELBO is an interesting direction for future work.

sections.heading: E.2 Joint versus Two-Phase Training
sections.text: Architectural differences. Table 10 summarizes the components of DiffPTS in Table 2 and of the hosts and their +DiffPTS variants in Table 4 . All +DiffPTS variants are trained end-to-end with the same joint objective as DiffPTS (Equation ( 14 )). Within each host, the architecture is held fixed and only the training procedure changes, namely the original two-phase or auxiliary training is replaced by joint ELBO training. DiffPTS in Table 2 deliberately inherits its f ϕ f_{\phi} and g ψ g_{\psi} architectures from NsDiff (a Non-stationary Transformer [ 39 ] and a three-layer MLP), so that the comparison against the two-phase baselines isolates the training objective rather than the architecture. D3U instead contributes a stronger patch-based mean backbone [ 43 ] , which is known to be particularly strong on the ETT datasets, and D3U+DiffPTS benefits from it. The gap between DiffPTS and D3U+DiffPTS on the ETT datasets is therefore architectural. The estimators themselves are not our contribution. Our contribution is how they should be trained, namely the ELBO itself prescribes a Gaussian NLL objective for whatever f ϕ f_{\phi} and g ψ g_{\psi} are chosen (Proposition 3.3 ), which is why the same objective improves every host. As summarized in Table 1 , D3U introduces no variance estimator. It diffuses the residual 𝐘 − f ϕ ​ ( 𝐗 ) \mathbf{Y}-f_{\phi}(\mathbf{X}) toward 𝒩 ⁡ ( 𝟎 , 𝐈 ) \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{I}) , which amounts to an implicit fixed unit variance in the residual space, whereas DiffPTS learns an input-dependent g ψ ​ ( 𝐗 ) g_{\psi}(\mathbf{X}) through the ELBO. Both methods estimate the conditional mean 𝔼 ⁡ [ 𝐘 ∣ 𝐗 ] \mathbb{E}[\mathbf{Y}\mid\mathbf{X}] with f ϕ f_{\phi} , and the difference lies in the training signal. D3U pretrains f ϕ f_{\phi} with a plain MSE and then freezes it, while DiffPTS trains f ϕ f_{\phi} jointly through the NLL term, whose squared error is weighted by 1 / g ψ ​ ( 𝐗 ) 1/g_{\psi}(\mathbf{X}) , so that f ϕ f_{\phi} allocates its capacity according to the predicted uncertainty. In addition, f ϕ f_{\phi} receives gradients from the denoising term, since 𝐘 t \mathbf{Y}_{t} in Equation ( 9 ) depends on it. These differences are visible in Figure 3 . The intervals of D3U and TMDM have a nearly constant width over time as a consequence of the missing variance estimator (Figure 3 (e-f)), while the intervals of DiffPTS track the empirical intervals (Figure 3 (a-b)), and Figure 3 (g) compares the estimated densities directly. Quantitatively, the calibration of the predictive distributions is reported as QICE in Table 5 , where DiffPTS is the best or second best on every dataset, while D3U suffers from its fixed-variance assumption.

sections.heading: E.3 Stationary versus Non-Stationary Datasets
sections.text: Intuition. When a dataset is near-stationary, the conditional mean and variance are stable functions of the input, so both estimators are easy to fit, and in the limit of a constant conditional variance, g ψ g_{\psi} degenerates toward the fixed-variance special case g ψ ≡ 1 g_{\psi}\equiv 1 of D3U and TMDM (Remark 13 ). Under non-stationarity, the location and scale that f ϕ f_{\phi} and g ψ g_{\psi} must track drift over time. Externally supervised targets, such as the sliding-window variance of NsDiff or the training residuals of RDIT, then become mis-specified, whereas the ELBO-prescribed NLL requires no external target and adapts the estimators to each input. A particularly favorable regime is periodic heteroscedastic data such as Solar and Traffic, where the variance changes strongly within a day yet is highly predictable from the input, which is where a learned g ψ ​ ( 𝐗 ) g_{\psi}(\mathbf{X}) helps most. Quantitative analysis. We compare each host with its own +DiffPTS variant using the full plug-and-play results in Table 8 , so that every method is measured against its own baseline. To classify the datasets, we standardize each dataset with the statistics of its training split, slide windows of length 168, and take the largest deviation across variates of the window mean from 0 (mean shift) and of the window variance from 1 (variance shift), since a single strongly drifting variate already requires non-stationary modeling. Splitting at the median yields a non-stationary group (Traffic, EXG, ILI, ECL, and ETTm2) and a stationary group (ETTh2, ETTm1, ETTh1, and Solar). Table 12 reports the relative CRPS improvement of +DiffPTS over each host. The gains of the ELBO objective are positive everywhere and consistently larger on the non-stationary group for all four hosts, in line with the intuition that externally supervised estimator targets are most mis-specified under distribution shift. sections.heading: E.5 Numerical Stability of the Gaussian NLL
sections.text: A very small g ψ ​ ( 𝐗 ) g_{\psi}(\mathbf{X}) might be expected to cause instability in the NLL term ( 𝐘 0 − f ϕ ​ ( 𝐗 ) ) 2 / g ψ ​ ( 𝐗 ) + log ⁡ g ψ ​ ( 𝐗 ) (\mathbf{Y}_{0}-f_{\phi}(\mathbf{X}))^{2}/g_{\psi}(\mathbf{X})+\log g_{\psi}(\mathbf{X}) . This term is, however, self-balancing. As g ψ g_{\psi} approaches zero, the quadratic term diverges, which prevents variance collapse, while the logarithmic term prevents the variance from blowing up. The implementation additionally uses a softplus output (Appendix B.2 ) and a small variance floor of 10 − 8 10^{-8} . Across all nine datasets, each with three seeds, we observed no NaN or divergence. Table 14 reports test-set statistics of the learned variance on ETTh1 and ETTm1. The learned g ψ g_{\psi} stays well bounded away from zero, whereas the hand-crafted alternative is the brittle one, in the sense that the sliding-window variance target of NsDiff degenerates toward zero on locally flat segments and its Gaussian NLL explodes there. This further supports learning g ψ g_{\psi} through the ELBO. sections.heading: E.6 Choice of the Number of Diffusion Steps
sections.text: Our choice of T = 20 T=20 follows the convention of prior diffusion forecasters [ 13 , 8 ] . In particular, TimeGrad [ 13 ] reports that its performance already saturates around T = 20 T=20 . We observe a similar saturation and further find that an overly large T T can even hurt performance, while a very small T T is only slightly worse (Table 15 ). T = 20 T=20 is the best on all datasets. We explain this behavior by answering two questions below. Table 15: CRPS of DiffPTS under different numbers of diffusion steps T T . All entries come from a separate set of runs under an identical configuration, so the T = 20 T=20 column may differ from Table 2 . Dataset T = 1 T=1 T = 20 T=20 T = 100 T=100 T = 1000 T=1000 ETTh1 0.387 0.377 0.432 0.552 ECL 0.232 0.218 0.259 0.498 ETTm2 0.284 0.274 0.353 0.554 EXG 0.307 0.275 0.320 0.639 Why T T can be much smaller for time series than for images. Each reverse transition is a small Gaussian-approximated correction. Images are very high-dimensional (e.g., 256 × 256 × 3 ≈ 2 × 10 5 256\times 256\times 3\approx 2\times 10^{5} dimensions) and their distributions are sharply multimodal, so many small steps are needed to fit them, typically around T = 1000 T=1000 [ 10 ] . Forecasting targets are far lower dimensional (e.g., 192 × 7 ≈ 1.3 × 10 3 192\times 7\approx 1.3\times 10^{3} dimensions on the ETT datasets, and TimeGrad even diffuses a single time step at a time). More importantly, the target is a conditional distribution in which the history 𝐗 \mathbf{X} and the target 𝐘 \mathbf{Y} are often highly similar, so the history already pins down most of the structure and leaves a close-to-unimodal conditional distribution to model. This also explains why TimeGrad, whose endpoint is a fixed 𝒩 ⁡ ( 𝟎 , 𝐈 ) \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{I}) , saturates at around T = 20 T=20 to 100 100 . The learned endpoint 𝒩 ⁡ ( f ϕ ​ ( 𝐗 ) , g ψ ​ ( 𝐗 ) ) \mathcal{N}(f_{\phi}(\mathbf{X}),g_{\psi}(\mathbf{X})) of DiffPTS shortens the path further by absorbing the location and scale, leaving only mild non-Gaussian structure to the reverse chain. This is visible in Figure 2 and Figure 3 (g), where the learned distribution differs from the Gaussian endpoint yet only mildly reshapes it and remains unimodal. Empirically, reducing T T from 20 to 1 on ETTh1 loses little (0.377 to 0.387), whereas removing the denoising entirely clearly degrades performance (0.374 to 0.437 in Table 3 ), confirming that only a small number of corrective steps is needed. Why T T should not be too large. We conjecture that the main cause lies in the balance between model complexity and data scarcity. A larger T T multiplies the model complexity, since the time-conditioned denoiser must fit T T distinct denoising sub-tasks and thus needs more data. Time series data are scarce (a single trajectory per dataset, e.g., fewer than 1000 steps on ILI), and under non-stationarity different regimes follow different distributions, which further reduces the effective sample size per regime. A large T T therefore increases the estimation burden without adding useful capacity, consistent with the degradation in Table 15 . In summary, the low-dimensional prediction target, the non-stationarity, and the data scarcity of time series forecasting jointly call for a compromise between a small and a large T T . The optimal T T is not known a priori, which is an interesting direction for future study, yet prior work [ 13 , 8 ] and our results suggest that a value around 20 is a good choice.

sections.heading: E.9 Limitations and Failure Cases
sections.text: Beyond the limitations discussed in Section 5 , we summarize the cases where DiffPTS helps less. First, the gains of the ELBO objective are marginal when a host’s estimators are already well specified, e.g., 0.8% CRPS for NsDiff on ETTh2 and ETTm2 (Table 12 ), and in the limit of a constant conditional variance, g ψ g_{\psi} degenerates toward the fixed-variance case g ψ ≡ 1 g_{\psi}\equiv 1 of D3U and TMDM. Second, DiffPTS is not uniformly the best on every metric. NsDiff attains a better QICE on ETTh2 and ILI (Table 5 ), which we attribute to its uncertainty-aware schedule when the sliding-window variance is a good approximation, and a few plug-and-play variants have a slightly higher MSE than their hosts on individual datasets, namely TMDM on ETTm2, D3U on EXG, and RDIT on Solar (Table 8 ). Third, the LSNM endpoint uses a diagonal covariance (Appendix E.1 ), we follow the simplified weighting of DDPM (Appendix E.4 ), and the number of diffusion steps is chosen empirically (Appendix E.6 ).

sections.text: 1. Claims Question: Do the main claims made in the abstract and introduction accurately reflect the paper’s contributions and scope? Answer: [Yes] Justification: Our claim is verified by Table 1 and Proposition 3.1 . Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the abstract and introduction do not include the claims made in the paper. • The abstract and/or introduction should clearly state the claims made, including the contributions made in the paper and important assumptions and limitations. Recently, Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Model (DDPM)-based approaches have shown promise by equipping the diffusion process with pretrained mean and variance estimators to accommodate distributional shift. However, these methods typically follow the standard DDPM framework and consider only partial components of the evidence lower bound (ELBO), treating the training of estimators as designed regression tasks separate from the variational inference framework. To address this, we rethink the ELBO under the Location-Scale Noise Model (LSNM) and find that it naturally induces a Gaussian negative log likelihood objective for the estimators and inherently defines a joint training objective that unifies recent diffusion paradigms for probabilistic forecasting. Building on this principled ELBO reformulation, we propose DiffPTS, a general framework that enables end-to-end optimization of all components within the ELBO. Across multiple benchmarks, DiffPTS consistently outperforms recent models, achieving state-of-the-art performance with an average CRPS/MSE reduction of over 14.53%/16.55% compared to existing diffusion-based methods. The code is available at https://github.com/wwy155/DiffPTS . 1 Introduction Probabilistic time series forecasting (PTSF) has become increasingly crucial in various real-world applications ranging from financial risk management [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] to climate prediction [ 4 , 5 ] . In particular, PTSF aims to effectively model the conditional distribution p ⁡ ( 𝐘 | 𝐗 ) p(\mathbf{Y}|\mathbf{X}) of future outcomes 𝐘 \mathbf{Y} given historical observations 𝐗 \mathbf{X} [ 6 ] . Given the dynamic nature of time series data, the fundamental challenge lies in accurately capturing complex and time-varying distributions [ 7 , 8 , 9 ] . In recent years, Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models (DDPMs) [ 10 , 11 ] have emerged as a powerful framework for modeling complex distributions, inspiring their growing adoption in probabilistic forecasting scenarios [ 12 , 13 , 14 ] . At their core, standard DDPMs optimize the Evidence Lower Bound (ELBO) to learn the data distribution by introducing a denoising network ϵ θ \epsilon_{\theta} that learns to predict the noise added during the forward diffusion process, enabling tractable variational inference from a fixed Gaussian endpoint p ⁡ ( 𝐘 T ) = 𝒩 ⁡ ( 𝟎 , 𝐈 ) p(\mathbf{Y}_{T})=\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{I}) . However, conventional DDPMs often fail in accurate probabilistic forecasting due to distributional shifts [ 8 , 15 , 16 ] . To address this limitation, recent approaches have proposed introducing adaptive mean and variance estimators ( f ϕ ​ ( 𝐗 ) f_{\phi}(\mathbf{X}) , OPEN g ψ ​ ( 𝐗 ) ) g_{\psi}(\mathbf{X})) into the diffusion process, either by designing a new residual-based denoising target ( 𝐘 − f ϕ ​ ( 𝐗 ) ) / g ψ ​ ( 𝐗 ) (\mathbf{Y}-f_{\phi}(\mathbf{X}))/g_{\psi}(\mathbf{X}) or by modifying the reverse diffusion endpoint to follow 𝒩 ⁡ ( f ϕ ​ ( 𝐗 ) , g ψ ​ ( 𝐗 ) ) \mathcal{N}(f_{\phi}(\mathbf{X}),g_{\psi}(\mathbf{X})) to accommodate distributional changes [ 8 , 17 ] , which have shown promising results [ 18 , 19 ] . Typically, these advancements follow the standard diffusion training paradigm, and the training of f ϕ f_{\phi} and g ψ g_{\psi} is conducted in separate pretraining stages or as auxiliary regression tasks by designing various targets for f ϕ f_{\phi} and g ψ g_{\psi} (e.g., NsDiff [ 8 ] uses a future sliding variance target for g ψ g_{\psi} ). These diverse design choices for training f ϕ f_{\phi} and g ψ g_{\psi} raise a critical question: How should f ϕ f_{\phi} and g ψ g_{\psi} be trained to best align with the DDPM within the variational inference framework? Motivated by this question, we rethink the ELBO and surprisingly find that when introducing adaptive estimators into the DDPM, crucial ELBO terms that were previously treated as constants become non-negligible and require explicit joint optimization. Specifically, the reconstruction non-denoising terms and prior matching terms must be strictly optimized to achieve a tight variational bound. Figure 1: Figure 1 illustrates the comparison of DDPM-based models on the ETTm1 dataset. The left panel displays the prediction intervals, while the right panel shows the corresponding endpoint distributions for TimeGrad, NsDiff, and DiffPTS (ours), respectively. Both TimeGrad and NsDiff utilize the standard ELBO objective from DDPM, whereas DiffPTS reformulates the ELBO to enable end-to-end training within a unified framework. Figure 1 presents a comparative analysis on the ETTm1 (Electricity Transformer Temperature, minutes) dataset, showcasing estimated prediction intervals (Left) and endpoint distributions (Right) across three diffusion-based models: TimeGrad [ 13 ] , NsDiff [ 8 ] , and our proposed DiffPTS. TimeGrad [ 13 ] follows the conventional DDPM framework with a fixed Gaussian prior, which fails to capture the temporal variability inherent in time series data. While NsDiff allows for dynamic mean and variance estimation by introducing the adaptive endpoint 𝒩 ⁡ ( f ⁡ ( 𝐗 ) , g ⁡ ( 𝐗 ) ) \mathcal{N}(f(\mathbf{X}),g(\mathbf{X})) , f ϕ , g ψ f_{\phi},g_{\psi} are considered as priors pretrained with designed losses that may not be inherently aligned with the diffusion process; as a result, the sliding variance target for g ψ g_{\psi} leads to an over-estimation in the uncertainty. Based on this observation, we rethink the ELBO under the Location-Scale Noise Model (LSNM) with estimators f ϕ , g ψ f_{\phi},g_{\psi} , and find that all three terms (reconstruction, denoise, prior matching) in the ELBO inherently require strict optimization, whereas two of them are largely discarded in recent methods. By reformulating the ELBO to explicitly incorporate these components, we establish a unified optimization objective that seamlessly integrates the training of estimators with the core diffusion training process. As in Figure 1 , DiffPTS optimizes these key components under the guidance of the core ELBO that is inherently required by the diffusion process, leading to a more accurate estimation (More explanation is given in Figure 3 ). In summary, our contributions are: 1) We identify a critical theoretical puzzle in recent advances for diffusion-based probabilistic forecasting: while trainable parameters are introduced to model distributional shift, they are not optimized within the diffusion ELBO framework. 2) We reformulate the diffusion ELBO to properly incorporate the introduced mean and variance estimators. Our analysis reveals that the ELBO inherently specifies a Gaussian negative log likelihood (NLL) objective for both estimators, indicating that prior approaches relying on manually designed targets may be fundamentally misaligned with the diffusion process. Moreover, we show that the ELBO provides a unified objective for both residual-based and endpoint-based methods. 3) Based on the reformulated ELBO, we propose DiffPTS, a novel end-to-end diffusion framework for PTSF. Extensive experiments demonstrate that DiffPTS consistently yields significant improvements in probabilistic forecasting performance. Notably, it outperforms previous diffusion-based baselines by over 14.53%/16.55% in CRPS/MSE across nine benchmarks, highlighting the importance of a full ELBO formulation. 2 Background 2.1 Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Model Diffusion probabilistic models [ 11 ] define a generative process by modeling the data distribution p ⁡ ( 𝐘 0 ) p(\mathbf{Y}_{0}) as the marginal of a joint distribution over a sequence of latent variables 𝐘 1 , … , 𝐘 T \mathbf{Y}_{1},\dots,\mathbf{Y}_{T} : p ( 𝐘 0 ) := ∫ p ( 𝐘 0 : T ) d 𝐘 1 : T p(\mathbf{Y}_{0}):=\int p(\mathbf{Y}_{0:T})\,d\mathbf{Y}_{1:T} . Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models (DDPMs) [ 10 ] construct the diffusion process based on a Markovian chain [ 20 ] : p ( 𝐘 0 : T ) := p ( 𝐘 T ) ∏ t = 1 T p ( 𝐘 t − 1 ∣ 𝐘 t ) p(\mathbf{Y}_{0:T}):=p(\mathbf{Y}_{T})\prod_{t=1}^{T}p(\mathbf{Y}_{t-1}\mid\mathbf{Y}_{t}) . In DDPM, the endpoint distribution is fixed to a Gaussian prior, i.e., p ⁡ ( 𝐘 T ) = 𝒩 ⁡ ( 𝟎 , 𝐈 ) p(\mathbf{Y}_{T})=\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{I}) . The model comprises two complementary processes: a forward process that progressively corrupts data by adding Gaussian noise, and a reverse (or denoising ) process that learns to recover the original data by iteratively removing noise [ 21 ] . The forward process is defined as: q ( 𝐘 1 : T ∣ 𝐘 0 ) \displaystyle q(\mathbf{Y}_{1:T}\mid\mathbf{Y}_{0}) : = ∏ t = 1 T q ⁡ ( 𝐘 t ∣ 𝐘 t − 1 ) , q ⁡ ( 𝐘 t ∣ 𝐘 t − 1 ) := 𝒩 ⁡ ( 𝐘 t , 1 − β t ​ 𝐘 t − 1 , β t ​ 𝐈 ) , \displaystyle:=\prod_{t=1}^{T}q(\mathbf{Y}_{t}\mid\mathbf{Y}_{t-1}),\quad q(\mathbf{Y}_{t}\mid\mathbf{Y}_{t-1}):=\mathcal{N}\big(\mathbf{Y}_{t};\sqrt{1-\beta_{t}}\,\mathbf{Y}_{t-1},\,\beta_{t}\mathbf{I}\big), (1) where β t ∈ ( 0 , 1 ) \beta_{t}\in(0,1) is a pre-specified noise schedule that controls the variance of added noise at each step. The reverse process involves denoising 𝐘 T \mathbf{Y}_{T} back to 𝐘 0 \mathbf{Y}_{0} and is parameterized by a learnable Gaussian transition kernel: p θ ​ ( 𝐘 t − 1 | 𝐘 t ) p_{\theta}(\mathbf{Y}_{t-1}|\mathbf{Y}_{t}) : p θ ​ ( 𝐘 t − 1 | 𝐘 t ) := 𝒩 ⁡ ( 𝐘 t − 1 , 𝝁 θ ​ ( 𝐘 t , t ) , 𝝈 θ ​ ( 𝐘 t , t ) ) , p_{\theta}(\mathbf{Y}_{t-1}|\mathbf{Y}_{t}):=\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{Y}_{t-1};\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\theta}(\mathbf{Y}_{t},t),\boldsymbol{\sigma}_{\theta}(\mathbf{Y}_{t},t)), (2) 𝝁 θ ​ ( 𝐘 t , t ) := 1 α t ​ ( 𝐘 t − β t 1 − α ¯ t ​ ϵ θ ​ ( 𝐘 t , t ) ) , 𝝈 θ ​ ( 𝐘 t , t ) = 1 − α ¯ t − 1 1 − α ¯ t ​ β t ​ 𝐈 , \boldsymbol{\mu}_{\theta}(\mathbf{Y}_{t},t):=\frac{1}{\sqrt{\alpha_{t}}}(\mathbf{Y}_{t}-\frac{\beta_{t}}{\sqrt{1-\bar{\alpha}_{t}}}\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{\theta}(\mathbf{Y}_{t},t)),\quad\boldsymbol{\sigma}_{\theta}(\mathbf{Y}_{t},t)=\frac{1-\bar{\alpha}_{t-1}}{1-\bar{\alpha}_{t}}\beta_{t}\mathbf{I}, (3) where α t := 1 − β t \alpha_{t}:=1-\beta_{t} , α ¯ t := ∏ i = 1 t α i \bar{\alpha}_{t}:=\prod_{i=1}^{t}\alpha_{i} , and ϵ θ ​ ( ⋅ , t ) \boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{\theta}(\cdot,t) denotes a neural network trained to predict the noise added at step t t . Training in DDPM is performed by maximizing a variational lower bound on the log-likelihood, known as the Evidence Lower Bound (ELBO) [ 15 , 22 ] : ELBO = 𝔼 q ⁡ ( 𝐘 1 ∣ 𝐘 0 ) [ log p θ ( 𝐘 0 ∣ 𝐘 1 ) ] − D KL ( q ( 𝐘 T ∣ 𝐘 0 ) ∥ p ( 𝐘 T ) ) \displaystyle=\;\mathbb{E}_{q(\mathbf{Y}_{1}\mid\mathbf{Y}_{0})}\left[\log p_{\theta}(\mathbf{Y}_{0}\mid\mathbf{Y}_{1})\right]-D_{\text{KL}}\big(q(\mathbf{Y}_{T}\mid\mathbf{Y}_{0})\,\|\,p(\mathbf{Y}_{T})\big) − ∑ t = 2 T 𝔼 q ⁡ ( 𝐘 t ∣ 𝐘 0 ) [ D KL ( q ( 𝐘 t − 1 ∣ 𝐘 t , 𝐘 0 ) ∥ p θ ( 𝐘 t − 1 ∣ 𝐘 t ) ) ] . \displaystyle-\sum_{t=2}^{T}\mathbb{E}_{q(\mathbf{Y}_{t}\mid\mathbf{Y}_{0})}\left[D_{\text{KL}}\big(q(\mathbf{Y}_{t-1}\mid\mathbf{Y}_{t},\mathbf{Y}_{0})\,\|\,p_{\theta}(\mathbf{Y}_{t-1}\mid\mathbf{Y}_{t})\big)\right]. (4) The first, second, and third terms in the ELBO objective are commonly referred to as the reconstruction , prior matching , and denoising terms, respectively. Crucially, in standard DDPM, the prior matching term is a KL divergence between two fixed distributions, which can be analytically computed and thus ignored during optimization [ 23 , 24 ] . Similarly, the reconstruction term involving q ⁡ ( 𝐘 0 | 𝐘 1 ) q(\mathbf{Y}_{0}|\mathbf{Y}_{1}) corresponds to a fixed distribution and can be reduced to the denoising term at t = 1 t=1 . As noted in [ 10 ] , p θ ​ ( ⋅ ) p_{\theta}(\cdot) can be reparameterized such that the dominant contribution to the loss arises from predicting the noise injected during the forward process. Consequently, the training objective simplifies to minimizing the following denoising loss: min θ ⁡ ℒ denoise ​ ( θ ) = 𝔼 𝐘 0 ∼ q ⁡ ( 𝐘 0 ) , ϵ ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 𝟎 , 𝐈 ) , t ∼ 𝒰 ⁡ { 1 , … , T } ​ [ ‖ ϵ 0 − ϵ θ ​ ( 𝐘 t , t ) ‖ 2 ] , \displaystyle\min_{\theta}\mathcal{L}_{\text{denoise}}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{Y}_{0}\sim q(\mathbf{Y}_{0}),\,\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{I}),\,t\sim\mathcal{U}\{1,\dots,T\}}\Big[\big\|\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{0}-\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{\theta}(\mathbf{Y}_{t},t)\big\|^{2}\Big], (5) where ϵ 0 ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 𝟎 , 𝐈 ) \boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{0}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{I}) and 𝐘 t = α ¯ t ​ 𝐘 0 + 1 − α ¯ t ​ ϵ 0 \mathbf{Y}_{t}=\sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_{t}}\,\mathbf{Y}_{0}+\sqrt{1-\bar{\alpha}_{t}}\,\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{0} is sampled directly via the reparameterization trick. At inference time, new samples are generated by first drawing 𝐘 T ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 𝟎 , 𝐈 ) \mathbf{Y}_{T}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{I}) and then iteratively applying the learned reverse process from t = T t=T down to t = 1 t=1 . 2.2 Probabilistic Time Series Forecasting Given a historical multivariate time series sample 𝐗 ∈ ℝ N × D \mathbf{X}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times D} , where N N denotes the look-back window length and D D the number of variables, the goal of probabilistic forecasting is to characterize the conditional distribution of the future trajectory p ( 𝐘 ) = { p ( 𝐲 1 ) , p ( 𝐲 2 ) , … , p ( 𝐲 M ) | 𝐲 ∈ ℝ D } p(\mathbf{Y})=\{p(\mathbf{y}_{1}),p(\mathbf{y}_{2}),...,p(\mathbf{y}_{M})|\mathbf{y}\in\mathbb{R}^{D}\} , where M M is the future window size. In this context, this DDPM framework is naturally extended to conditional DDPM [ 25 ] , which incorporates past observations 𝐗 \mathbf{X} as an additional conditioning variable, and the conditional DDPM is formulated as: p θ ( 𝐘 0 : T | 𝐗 ) := p ( 𝐘 T | 𝐗 ) ∏ t = 1 T p θ ( 𝐘 t − 1 ∣ 𝐘 t , 𝐗 ) , p_{\theta}(\mathbf{Y}_{0:T}|\mathbf{X}):=p(\mathbf{Y}_{T}|\mathbf{X})\prod_{t=1}^{T}p_{\theta}(\mathbf{Y}_{t-1}\mid\mathbf{Y}_{t},\mathbf{X}), (6) p θ ​ ( 𝐘 t − 1 ∣ 𝐘 t , 𝐗 ) := 𝒩 ⁡ ( 𝐘 t − 1 , 𝝁 θ ​ ( 𝐘 t , 𝐗 , t ) , 𝝈 θ ​ ( 𝐘 t , 𝐗 , t ) ) . p_{\theta}(\mathbf{Y}_{t-1}\mid\mathbf{Y}_{t},\mathbf{X}):=\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{Y}_{t-1};\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\theta}(\mathbf{Y}_{t},\mathbf{X},t),\boldsymbol{\sigma}_{\theta}(\mathbf{Y}_{t},\mathbf{X},t)). (7) The reverse transition is typically parameterized by incorporating an additional conditioning input to the denoising network: ϵ θ ​ ( ⋅ , t , 𝐗 ) \boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{\theta}(\cdot,t;\mathbf{X}) . Beyond this parameterization, several studies [ 12 , 13 , 14 ] have proposed mechanisms to incorporate various conditional information, e.g., mixed historical codes, into the reverse process to better guide the denoising function. Notably, both the ELBO (Equation ( 4 )) and the simplified denoising loss (Equation ( 5 )) retain their original form in these methods. Nevertheless, PTSF poses unique challenges due to strong temporal dependencies [ 26 , 27 , 28 ] , non-stationarity [ 7 , 29 ] , and input-dependent uncertainty [ 21 , 30 ] . While diffusion models have shown promise in this domain [ 12 , 13 ] , the conventional paradigm, diffusing raw observations 𝐘 \mathbf{Y} toward a standard Gaussian prior, often overlooks the input-dependent nature of predictive uncertainty [ 31 , 32 ] . We summarize existing approaches and find that, despite introducing auxiliary estimators, these components are not dictated by the standard ELBO and are instead added heuristically. Based on this observation, we argue that a proper variational objective should explicitly govern the form and role of these estimators. To this end, we derive a corrected evidence lower bound that imposes precise requirements on the introduced estimators, ensuring a tighter variational bound. Building on this formulation, we present DiffPTS , a novel probabilistic forecasting framework trained in an end-to-end joint optimization scheme and we describe its training and sampling algorithms. 3.1 The Missing Puzzle of The ELBO Recent diffusion-based approaches for probabilistic time series forecasting have achieved notable success. Following previous work [ 8 , 33 ] , we evaluate on nine real-world datasets: ETT {h1, h2, m1, m2}, Electricity (ECL), Influenza-like Illness (ILI), Exchange Rate (EXR), Traffic, and Solar Energy (Solar). All experiments adopt a input sequence length of 168 time steps, ILI uses 32 prediction steps, and other datasets follow 192 prediction steps. Data splits follow domain conventions: ETT datasets use 12/4/4-month partitions for training, validation, and testing; all other datasets employ a chronological 7:1:2 split ratio. We provide dataset details in Appendix B.1 . Baselines . We select eight recent strong PTSF baselines for comparison, including TimeGrad [ 13 ] , CSDI [ 12 ] , TimeDiff [ 14 ] , TMDM [ 33 ] , DiffusionTS [ 35 ] , D3U [ 16 ] , RDIT [ 17 ] , NsDiff [ 8 ] . Specifically, TimeGrad, CSDI, TimeDiff, DiffusionTS follow the standard diffusion paradigm; TMDM, D3U, RDIT, NsDiff introduce estimators into diffusion process through two phases pretraining. Implementation . All experiments are conducted under popular long-term multivariate probabilistic forecasting settings [ 8 , 33 ] . We run all experiments with seeds { 1 , 2 , 3 } \{1,2,3\} for 10 epochs and select the best model based on the validation performance for final test evaluation. The learning rate is set to 0.001, batch size to 32, and the number of timesteps T = 20 T=20 , consistent with prior work [ 8 , 13 ] . We employ a linear noise schedule with β 1 = 10 − 4 \beta^{1}=10^{-4} and β T = 0.02 \beta^{T}=0.02 , in line with the setup used in conventional DDPM [ 10 ] . We use Adam optimizer [ 36 ] and the experiments were all performed using an NVIDIA RTX A6000 GPU. In inference, we generate 100 samples to estimate the distribution [ 37 , 38 ] . For the baseline models, we utilize their default parameters. For implementation of f ϕ f_{\phi} and g ψ g_{\psi} , we follow previous work [ 8 , 33 ] to use Non-stationary Transformer [ 39 ] and a three-layer linear model [ 40 , 41 ] , respectively. More details are provided in Appendix B.2 . Metrics . Following prior work’s metric settings [ 8 , 13 , 33 ] , we use Continuous Ranked Probability Score (CRPS) [ 42 ] and mean square error (MSE) to validate the performance of the estimated uncertainty quantification and point forecasting performance. For both metrics, smaller values indicate better performance. Detailed formula is provided in Appendix B.3 . 4.2 Main Experiments The experimental results are presented in Table 2 .
